item.title: The solution to societal problems
item.description:
Being richer solves a lot of problems.
This should seem obvious but all too many act as if it isn't.
Simply because we're humans, we'd find things to worry about.
If everyone in Bangladesh were on Tk100,00 a month, there would still be problems but they'd all be very different problems from those currently on Tk2,000.
Being rich means that we simply do not have the problems of the poor.
Sure, we might then have rich people problems, but as I say, they're different ones.
That we will still have problems even if we're all rich is just one of those human things. Humans are like that. There's even an internet meme about it: “First world problems” which can be rather fun to look up.
This is not just a philosophic observation, it's something important for us as we direct our efforts into making the world a better place.
There are indeed myriad problems that the poor have. But should we solve each of those problems, one by one, or just go for the economic growth that makes the poor rich and thereby solve those poor people problems?
An example of this is a piece in this newspape r . There are stories of how bad the poor have had it from the floods around Chittagong -- I believe them all. For it always is the poor who find their lives made worse -- more worse perhaps -- by disasters and other vilenesses.
Something mentioned repeatedly is access to menstrual products. OK, yes, this is a real problem. And yet part of the solution seems to be “ensuring dignified menstrual hygiene management” and that's where I disagree.
Yes, I grasp the point. When my wife and I lived in Soviet Russia, one of the supplies I bought in England to bring back to her was packs of tampons to deal with exactly this.
However, at a societal level, I disagree. The point is not to provide menstrual products to poor people. It's to not have people so poor that menstrual products are a problem.
That is, grow the economy, make the poor rich, and this problem, along with any others, simply vanishes into the general wealth of the society.
This does in fact happen. While there are still political campaigns about it and so on, the reality is this has been solved in any and all of the rich countries.
It's simply a matter of fact that a supermarket-brand box of 24 tampons costs a pound in Britain. That is five minutes work at the current minimum wage of £12 an hour in that same country.
Something that is available in hundreds of variations in tens of thousands of shops across the country at the price of five minutes minimum wage work just isn't a societal problem any more.
That's one that has been solved by people becoming rich.
This is true of many of the problems of poverty. They're solved by not being poor any more.
So, the societal effort should be toward solving poverty itself through economic growth. For that then, in and of itself, solves all those other problems.
This is true of housing, of nutrition, of having a few changes of clothes, of medical care, of education and yes, it's even a cure for gender discrimination -- rich people don't depend upon muscle power to make a living. Therefore, men do not control household incomes the way they do in nations such as Bangladesh.
Most of the things we don't like about poverty are caused by poverty itself, not other issues. Therefore the solution for the problems of poverty is the economic growth that abolishes poverty.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: The exchange rate ate our start-ups
item.description:
Every founder in Dhaka has a version of the same story. You raise dollars and you spend in taka.
You grow, sometimes fast, and then you sit across from your investor two years later and watch them do arithmetic that has nothing to do with anything you built.
I have been on both sides of that table. It took me too long to understand that the number that killed the most Bangladeshi start-ups was never in the pitch deck.
When foreign money first came into this market in 2016/17, the rate was around Tk84 to the dollar. It is now above Tk122. That is a 45% hole in the floor of every company earning revenue in taka and reporting to a fund that raised in dollars.
Now put venture math on top. PE and VC investors underwrite returns of 40-60%. So a company selling to Bangladeshi customers has to clear that hurdle and climb out of the currency hole before the investor sees a single point of return.
You are not being asked to build a good company. You are being asked to build a great one and then pay a 45% tax on the outcome for reasons no operator here controls.
Most of us cannot do it.
Look at the wreckage. Funding peaked at $434 million in 2021. In the first half of 2026 it was $6m. Six, across six deals, in a country of 170 million people.
Investment per capita is 70 cents against India's nine dollars, at nearly identical GDP per capita.
Global venture funding recovered to $469 billion in 2025. The world reopened its wallet and Bangladesh got nothing. Whatever happened to us was not a global winter. It was local.
Local money never cushioned any of it. In all of 2025, financial institutions, domestic investors, or angel investors barely put in any money in Bangladeshi start-ups. In the first half of 2026, 100% of the capital was foreign.
The second half of the trap? There is nowhere to sell. No investor commits to a market they cannot leave.
Which brings me to the listing venue for small companies in Bangladesh: The DSE SME platform opened in September 2021 under the Qualified Investor Offer rules, letting small-capital companies raise from investors holding at least Tk 50 lakh in the market.
It went live with six companies: A feed mill, an agro processor, a biscuit maker, a toy manufacturer, a weaving mill, a chemicals firm.
Five years on, that is still roughly the profile. Our technology sector has produced perhaps a dozen companies of real scale and not one of them has gone near the SME board.
The reason is that a venture-funded start-up burning capital to buy growth has no audited profit to show a qualified investor, and no story that ends anywhere except another foreign round.
We built companies structurally incapable of using the one exit our own market offers.
That is fixable, and it points at the same answer the currency does.
If a weakening taka destroys returns for companies earning in taka, it hands those returns to companies earning in dollars and spending in taka.
Same currency move, opposite sign. Every year the taka slips, an export business gets cheaper to run and its revenue buys more at home.
AI data and evaluation work. Engineering and design sold abroad. Software priced in dollars for foreign customers. Payroll in Dhaka. These businesses sidestep repatriation, because the money is already offshore.
They can reach profitability without a buyer existing. And profitability is precisely what makes a company listable on the SME board, which is how a domestic exit market gets built rather than waited for.
I am not saying abandon the consumer market. I am saying stop pretending the last cycle failed on execution alone.
We built taka companies on dollar capital. The next generation should do the opposite.
Hussain M Elius is the co-founder of Pathao and Wind.App (exited to Fin, Inc), and author of “Moving Bangladesh: The Origin Story of Pathao.”

item.title: TIE-ITET Innovation & Research Cell to increase competitiveness of textile, apparel industries
item.description:
Textile Innovation Exchange (TIE) and The Institution of Textile Engineers and Technologists (ITET), Bangladesh, have signed an In-Collaboration Agreement to establish the TIE–ITET Innovation & Research Cell, creating a structured platform to connect textile professionals, industry, researchers and innovators, accelerate practical innovation, and bring those innovations to Textile Innovation Expo 2026, scheduled for November 12–14, 2026 at International Convention City Bashundhara (ICCB), Dhaka.
The collaboration was announced at an MoU signing ceremony at Dhaka Regency Hotel on August 20. Under the agreement, ITET will be recognized as an “In-Collaboration” partner of TIE and will support the Expo by mobilizing textile engineers and technologists, factories, industry leaders, policymakers, public institutions, exhibitors, sponsors and other relevant stakeholders. TIE will continue to own and lead the Textile Innovation Expo.
The agreement was signed on behalf of Textile Innovation Exchange by Engr. Ehsanul Karim Kaiser, Chairman, TIE, and on behalf of ITET by Engr. Md. Enayet Hossain, President, ITET.
The Expo is already generating strong momentum across the industry, with Pacific RSF Associates Ltd. and a growing list of leading local and international companies confirming participation to showcase their latest innovations, technologies and solutions.
Unlike conventional trade expos, Textile Innovation Expo 2026 is being positioned as a leading innovation platform, where live demonstrations, applied technologies, factory-ready solutions and sustainability-driven innovations take center stage.
The Expo will feature four concurrent innovation zones - Dyeing & Printing Innovation Expo, Textile Materials Innovation Expo, Garments Automation & Innovation Expo, and Green & SusTech Expo - bringing together a wide spectrum of technologies, materials, automation systems and sustainable solutions under one roof.
With increasing participation from solution providers, machinery innovators, chemical and material companies, automation leaders and sustainability-focused organizations, the Expo is expected to become one of the largest and most dynamic textile innovation gatherings in the region.
At the signing ceremony, Engr. ASM Hafizur Rahman Nixon, Secretary General, ITET, and Engr. Sumayel Muhammad Mallik, Senior Vice President, ITET, Prof. Dr. Engr. A N M Ahmed Ullah, Head of the Department of Textile Engineering, Southeast University, Nafis-Ud-Doula, Director, BGMEA & Director, Impress-Newtex Composite Textiles Ltd. shared their perspectives on the growing importance of innovation for the competitiveness and future of Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry.
ASM Tareq Amin, Member Secretary, TIE, presented the overall activities, mission and vision of Textile Innovation Exchange and outlined the future activities planned under the TIE–ITET collaboration. He highlighted how the partnership can connect industry professionals and institutions with practical innovation, applied research, capability development and the Textile Innovation Expo.
ATM Mahbubul Alam Milton, Executive Director of Masco Group and Member of the Steering Board, TIE, emphasized that innovation has become essential for the survival and competitiveness of the textile industry.
Engr. Md. Enayet Hossain, President, ITET, said the agreement reflects the organization’s commitment to moving beyond institutional discussion and delivering visible activities for textile engineers and the wider industry.

item.title: Rajshahi residents suffer as flyover projects move at a snail’s pace
item.description:
Construction work of four flyovers in Rajshahi city has been progressing at a slow pace, with none completed even after the project deadline expired in June this year. The prolonged construction has caused inconvenience to residents, while roads around the project sites have been left riddled with potholes, mud and stagnant rainwater.
Residents complain that slow progress, poor coordination and inadequate supervision have turned the development projects into a source of public suffering. During the monsoon, several roads around the construction sites become nearly unusable, increasing the risk of accidents and traffic congestion.
Rajshahi City Corporation (RCC), however, says payment-related complications have been resolved and construction is now moving ahead. The city authority expects two to three flyovers to be opened to traffic by the end of this year.
According to RCC sources, construction of the four flyovers began in late 2023 at a cost of Tk 540 crore to ease traffic congestion at major railway crossings. The projects include the Raypara flyover at Tk 86.19 crore, Bandhgate at Tk 97.70 crore, Bilshimla at Tk 87.30 crore and the largest flyover at Shaheed AHM Kamaruzzaman Square at Tk 270.51 crore.
The deadline for completing three of the flyovers has been extended to December this year, while the deadline for the largest project is being extended to June 2028.
Kamaruzzaman Square flyover has been particularly controversial. Following the fall of the Awami League government, local residents and businesspeople staged demonstrations and submitted memoranda questioning the necessity of the project.
A recent visit to the area found construction of the flyover from Bindur Mor to New Market still at the pillar-construction stage. Partial closure of the important road has caused frequent traffic congestion around the Railgate area.
Businessman Abdur Rahim said the slow pace of construction had severely affected his business. “For nearly six months, there has been almost no business,” he said.
Rickshaw driver Zahidul Islam said potholes and damaged roads were frequently causing vehicle breakdowns. Residents of Bandhgate and Baharampur said road closures were forcing vehicles to take longer routes, wasting both time and fuel.
Majid Sons Executive Director Jargisur Rahman said 75-80% of Bilshimla flyover work had been completed and expressed hope that the project would be finished by December.
RCC Acting Executive Engineer Ahmad Al Moin said three flyovers were expected to be completed by the end of the year. He said Kamaruzzaman Square project was facing various complications and its deadline was being extended until mid-2028.
RCC Administrator Mahfuzur Rahman Riton said payment-related complications had previously slowed construction but had now been resolved. Contractors have been instructed to complete the projects within the revised deadlines.

item.title: ‘Reconciliation’ in manifestos, absent from discussions
item.description:
Several political parties had pledged in their manifestos for the 13th parliamentary election to form a Truth and Reconciliation Commission to resolve conflict, discord and divisions in the country. The initiative was intended to establish a forward-looking political culture and reconciliation in place of a politics of vengeance and retaliation.

However, six months have passed since the parliamentary election, and no such commission has been formed. There has not even been any discussion of the issue in parliament or in the political arena.

A review of the election manifestos shows that the BNP, Jamaat-e-Islami and National Citizen Party (NCP) pledged to establish such a commission in the latest national election. The BNP and Jamaat-e-Islami called it a Truth and Healing Commission, while the NCP pledged to establish a Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Earlier, in its manifesto for the 11th parliamentary election in 2018, the Jatiya Oikya Front had pledged to form an “all-party truth-finding and reconciliation commission.”

Political parties say the government has been in office for six months and there is still time. Besides, the Awami League, whose activities are currently banned, has not yet admitted to any wrongdoing. Instead, the party continues to issue threats. Under such circumstances, they say, it is not possible to form such a commission.

Political analysts say the interim government had also talked about such a commission. Various political parties subsequently included similar pledges in their manifestos. But these remain merely “words on paper.” No one appears to be taking them seriously.

The context behind the pledges

During the 1971 Liberation War, crimes against humanity, including rape, torture and genocide, were committed against the people of this land. Some people from this territory collaborated with the Pakistanis in the destruction. Later, during the rule of various governments, including the Awami League, many people were subjected to enforced disappearance, killings and torture. In July and August 2024, the people of this land again became victims of serious abuses, killings, genocide and other crimes against humanity.

Following the July mass uprising, the interim government banned the Awami League’s activities, a ban that remains in force. Many of the party’s leaders and activists are in hiding, while others have left the country. Social divisions have existed in Bangladesh since its birth and have become increasingly pronounced over time. Against this backdrop, various quarters have been calling for a Truth and Reconciliation Commission primarily to end violence and build national unity.

Where do the three major political parties stand on reconciliation?

Political pledges

The interim government was formed after the fall of the Awami League government in the mass uprising of 5 August, 2024. During the interim government’s tenure, a discussion was held at the Judicial Administration Training Institute on 10 May, 2025, on the second draft of the Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Ordinance, 2025. Poet and political thinker Farhad Mazhar said at the meeting, “If you try to prosecute those involved in these disappearances, this interim government will not sustain. That is the reality.… We have to look at the experiences of other countries and see how they resolved this. They resolved it by setting up a separate commission through a Truth and Justice Commission.”

At the meeting, then interim government Law Adviser Asif Nazrul also spoke about forming a Truth and Reconciliation Commission. He said the government would establish such a commission. This nation will not be liberated by fighting among ourselves forever, he said adding, stressing the need to build national unity.

He also said it would probably have been better if such an initiative had existed since 1972. Those responsible for heinous crimes such as genocide and crimes against humanity are not very numerous, he said, and they must be appropriately punished. He added that the commission should be formed, among other reasons, to establish that those perpetrators had become alienated from the mainstream of the nation.

To gain experience about Truth and Reconciliation Commissions, then Chief Justice Syed Refaat Ahmed and then Law Adviser Asif Nazrul visited South Africa in May that year. The interim government, however, did not take the matter any further.

Pledges from three parties

In its manifesto for the 13th parliamentary election held on February 12, the BNP pledged to establish a Truth and Healing Commission. It said, “The BNP wants to establish a new, forward-looking political culture in place of a politics of vengeance and retaliation. The BNP believes nation-building means not merely running the state, but also building a common national identity by overcoming divisions. Ending political and social divisions on the basis of Bangladeshi nationalism—our one identity is that we are all Bangladeshis.”

Jamaat-e-Islami, which also pledged to establish a Truth and Healing Commission, said in its manifesto that a task force would be formed for this purpose with representation from various sections of Bangladeshi society and technical assistance from the United Nations. Through this initiative, the party said, the truth about human rights violations committed over the past 15 years would be uncovered and a new chapter would be opened for the nation.

The NCP said in its manifesto that exemplary punishment would be ensured for all crimes against humanity committed during the period of “Awami fascism,” including the genocide, the Shapla massacre, the BDR killings, enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings. It also pledged to establish a Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

Such a commission had also been proposed earlier as a means of establishing national unity. In its manifesto for the 11th parliamentary election in 2018, the Jatiya Oikya Front said, “The goal is national unity, not vengeance or vindictiveness.” It said that over the previous 10 years, unimaginable authoritarianism and the use of police as party cadres had resulted in thousands of false cases, enforced disappearances, killings, extortion through cases and extrajudicial killings, leaving hundreds of thousands of families angry and devastated. To resolve these problems and establish social peace, the alliance pledged to form an “all-party truth-finding and reconciliation commission” comprising eminent academics, social workers and lawyers. It said the commission would seek to resolve harassment cases filed against political opponents through open discussions, forgiveness and compensation.

At the time, the Jatiya Oikya Front was formed under the leadership of Dr Kamal Hossain, bringing together the BNP, Gono Forum, JSD and Nagorik Oikya. The Krishak Sramik Janata League later joined the alliance. The Oikya Front emerged as a major opposition alliance in that election, although it became inactive after the election.

Why Bangladesh needs reconciliation

What are the political parties saying now?

An attempt was made to find out what political parties currently think about a Truth and Reconciliation Commission. BNP Acting Secretary General and Prime Minister’s Political Adviser Ruhul Kabir Rizvi recently told Prothom Alo that the formation of a Truth and Healing Commission is included in the BNP’s election manifesto. It was included after careful consideration. The BNP is moving ahead with implementing its other manifesto pledges, he said, adding that this one would also be implemented gradually.

Parliament has seen discussions on many issues so far. Why, then, has there been no discussion about forming a Truth and Healing Commission? Asked about this, Rizvi said he is not a member of parliament. “I cannot say why those who are MPs have not raised the issue yet,” he said.

Jamaat-e-Islami had said it would establish such a commission if it came to power. The party’s Secretary General Mia Golam Parwar told Prothom Alo that Jamaat-e-Islami would undertake many initiatives if entrusted with running the government, as outlined in its manifesto. This is one of those initiatives that cannot be undertaken without being in government. Asked why the issue had not been discussed in parliament, Mia Golam Parwar said only one parliamentary session had taken place. “Everything is not over yet. We have to be patient and see what happens,” he said.

NCP Joint Convener Sarwar Tushar told Prothom Alo that they have spoken about a Truth and Reconciliation Commission and continue to do so at various times. But the Awami League is still carrying out sporadic attacks, setting fire to places including July memorials, issuing threats, creating security risks and describing July as a conspiracy. If they continue doing these things, Truth and Reconciliation is not possible.

Noting that Truth and Reconciliation begins with an admission of wrongdoing, Sarwar Tushar said the Awami League would have to acknowledge its mistakes. That is the first step. Nothing is possible before that. But anything like that is yet to be seen. There are still groups supporting the Awami League in society, he noted, adding that if they want the Awami League to return to politics, the party would first have to say that it acknowledges its mistakes.

Experiences from other countries

Various countries around the world have established commissions to uncover the truth and restore relationships after prolonged conflicts, as part of efforts to establish peace and make democratic transitions. South Africa is one such country. After more than 300 years of racial rule, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, or TRC, played a crucial role in establishing democratic governance in South Africa.

The apartheid system was introduced in South Africa in 1948. From then on, anti-apartheid organisations, including the African National Congress (ANC), intensified their movements. At one point, the ANC launched an armed struggle.

The ANC was led by Nelson Mandela, the undisputed leader of the anti-apartheid movement. After 27 years in prison, he was released by the government on 11 February, 1990, amid national and international pressure. However, white minority and apartheid rule remained in place. His release therefore marked the beginning of a difficult road ahead.

Mandela focused on protecting the rights of all from the very day of his release, setting aside thoughts of revenge, as recounted in his autobiography Long Walk to Freedom. Mandela wrote that after being released from prison after 27 years, his convoy travelled to Cape Town via rural roads to avoid the unexpected crowds. Having heard the news on the radio, many white families stood along those roads to welcome him. Some raised their clenched right fists in salute. Mandela was surprised by the show of solidarity from the white families.

At one point, Mandela stopped the convoy and thanked one white family, saying that their support had greatly inspired him. The experience made him realise that he was entering a South Africa very different from the country he had left behind when he went to prison. That same day, Mandela delivered a historic speech at Cape Town City Hall, conveying a message of peace, democracy and freedom for all.

Truth and Reconciliation Commission to be formed: Asif Nazrul

South Africa’s TRC: a new model

Nelson Mandela became president in South Africa’s first democratic election in 1994. In 1995, his government enacted legislation on the promotion of national unity and reconciliation, under which the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, or TRC, was established that same year.

Seventeen commissioners were appointed to the TRC. An independent selection panel comprising representatives of all political parties, civil society and religious organisations selected the commissioners through public interviews. The president appointed the chairperson and deputy chairperson of the commission.

The commissioners were tasked with investigating human rights violations committed between 1960 and 1994, hearing testimony from victims, granting amnesty to perpetrators, producing an impartial historical record and developing policies for compensation. Three committees were formed to fulfil these objectives: the Human Rights Violations Committee, the Reparation and Rehabilitation Committee, and the Amnesty Committee.

The TRC received more than 22,000 written complaints from people who had suffered persecution. These complaints revealed serious human rights violations during apartheid, including torture, killings, disappearances, abductions and extreme acts of inhumanity. Hearings involving victims and perpetrators were held publicly.

More than 7,000 applications for amnesty were submitted to the TRC. Hearings were held on more than 2,500 of them, and nearly 1,500 applicants were granted amnesty. The South African TRC published its first report in 1998, revealing the truth about human rights violations during the apartheid era.

Because it included provisions for amnesty for past crimes, South Africa’s TRC differed from the Nuremberg trials. The Nuremberg trials, it may be noted, prosecuted senior Nazi officials in Germany after World War II. Following the success of the commission, black and white South Africans have continued to live alongside one another while avoiding conflict.

South Africa’s TRC came to be recognised internationally as a new model. Subsequently, many countries established TRCs to promote peace and democracy, including Sierra Leone, Liberia, Canada, Argentina, Chile, Ghana, Guatemala, Peru, East Timor and Morocco.

There is also an example at home

While Truth and Reconciliation Commissions have been widely established in other countries in response to mass killings and torture, Bangladesh once established a similar commission to rehabilitate corrupt individuals in society.

After a military-backed caretaker government took office in January 2007, it launched an anti-corruption drive. Around 70,000 people were arrested and detained in prison at the time for corruption and various other social offences. Against this backdrop, the then government established the Truth and Accountability Commission, or Truth Commission, on 30 July, 2008.

The three-member commission, headed by former justice Habibur Rahman Khan, had a five-month mandate. Corrupt individuals would appear before the commission and confess to their offences. They would then deposit their illicit money, or a specified portion of it, into the state treasury. They would subsequently be granted amnesty, while their identities were kept confidential.

However, following a writ petition, the High Court declared the Truth Commission illegal on 13 November, 2008. The Awami League government that subsequently came to power also did not recognise the commission. On 1 April, 2009, then Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina disclosed in parliament a list of 448 people who had confessed before the Truth Commission and received exemption from liability for corruption.

In other words, the commission was an attempt to rehabilitate those individuals in society by granting them amnesty and freeing them from corruption charges.

Difficult to move forward without healing the wounds

Professor Anu Muhammad, a member of the Democratic Rights Committee, said if violence continues in the country and grievances remain unresolved, these things create uncertainty and instability in society in the long term. He said such grievances are passed down from generation to generation. Hatred, hostility and vengeance create a crisis of thought and empathy in society.

“That is why a solution is needed. We need to uncover the truth and reach a point of reconciliation.”

Various political parties have been talking about this issue, he said, and the interim government also spoke about it. But these remain merely words. No one seems to be taking the matter seriously.

Anu Muhammad believes everything needs to be resolved. Society accumulates many historical wounds over time. If we do not heal all these historical wounds, it will be difficult to move forward.

item.title: Bodies of former Rangpur zilla school teacher, wife and 2 children recovered
item.description:
The bodies of retired Rangpur Zilla School teacher Ganapati Chakraborty, his wife and their son and daughter were recovered from a three-storey building in Kamal Kachhna Machuapara village in Rangpur city.

Local residents and police discovered the bodies at around 8:30 pm on Saturday.

The Criminal Investigation Department (CID) and metropolitan police have cordoned off the building.

The deceased were identified as Ganapati Chakraborty, 65, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty, 50, their son Ayush Chakraborty, 14, and daughter Agami Chakraborty, 28.

Rangpur CID police inspector Abu Hasan Kabir confirmed the recovery of the four bodies. He said a bad smell had spread throughout the building.

Police suspect that someone killed the family. The entire family lived on the second floor of the building.

Officer-in-Charge (OC) of Kotwali police station AKM Nazmul Kader said the murders were believed to have taken place two or three days ago.

Rangpur CID officer-in-charge Sumit Chowdhury inspected the scene and told journalists at around 1:00 am, “From what we have seen so far, it appears to be a robbery. It seems the incident took place three or four days ago. The house’s electricity connection had been disconnected. Everything where money was kept had been broken. It appears that they were killed by strangling around their necks.”

item.title: Raven for recreation: Premium games at pleasing prices
item.description:
The sharp click of balls, occasional cheer after a well-played shot and the lively chatter of friends creating a lively atmosphere. From one corner comes the sound of a competitive game, while another, friends exchange jokes and playful remarks between turns. The mix of laughter, conversation and the steady sounds of games create a vibrant atmosphere, giving visitors a chance to take a break from their daily routine and spend time together.

Indoor gaming has become a popular way of spending leisure time among young people in Dhaka. Gaming and recreational zones have added to the city's growing options for indoor entertainment.

The gaming lounge I recently visited in Mirpur DOHS Gate-1, however, offered something somewhat different than those regular gaming places. It was not just another regular digital amusement gaming centre.

It brought together traditional table-and-cue sports such as billiards, snooker, pools etc. that are more commonly found in five-star hotels, luxury clubs or exclusive recreational spaces in the capital, while keeping the cost within reach of common.

This place is Raven, which has been operating for around a year and a half.

The setup really looks like an expensive recreational zone of a club. Billiards, snooker and pool tables occupy the main lounge, while a separate room is also dedicated to PlayStation 5 for FIFA (football simulation game) and racing games, for the people interested in digital games.

This division gives each type of game its own space, allowing a group of friends to settle into their own interest.

The interior is bright and attractive, with sufficient lighting for players and neatly arranged equipment. The place is also clean and well maintained.

It has the appearance of a relatively upscale gaming lounge, although its pricing is considerably less than what one might expect from such a setting.

The pricing is perhaps one of the biggest reason to attract customers. The hourly rates range from just only Tk 8 to Tk 15 for different tables! Quite a rate of course for enjoying the games over a long period.

The prices of PlayStation 5 for racing and FIFA games are comparatively higher, given that they are console games, but the rates remain accessible for groups of friends when the cost is shared among several players.

That affordability is perhaps the main reason behind Raven's growing popularity.

During our visit, students made up a significant part of the crowd. Some came in groups to play after classes, while others said they spend several hours there during holidays.

The venue also has regular customers from the corporate and business community, particularly those interested in these games.

One student, who visits Raven regularly with friends, said the friendly staff and affordable rates keep bringing them back.

The student said, "The staffs are very friendly and helpful, and the place is not as expensive as other gaming spots. That is why we come here almost every day. On holidays, we sometimes stay here for the whole day to play."

For some visitors, Raven has become a way to disconnect from the stress of work. A businessman who regularly visits the lounge said he particularly enjoys playing after office hours. "During the day, I am busy with work, but at night, this is a place where I feel my workload disappears. I have a great interest in snooker and pool, so after work I come straight here to play," he said.

The manager also spoke about the atmosphere at Raven. He said, "It does not even feel like hard work. The owners are very friendly, and as people come here to enjoy themselves, there is always a pleasant atmosphere."

The story behind the place became even more interesting when we met its owner.

As I looked around the place and spoke to some of the visitors, I casually asked about the owner to the manager. A staff member told me that he was in his office and went to call him. To my surprise, a teenage boy soon walked out and politely asked if there was anything I needed.

When I asked if he was the owner, he simply nodded. Seeing the place, its setup and the people who had gathered there, I had expected someone considerably older to be behind the business. My curiosity grew, and I wanted to know more about how such a place came into being.

I sat down with him for a conversation, and his enthusiasm about the gaming lounge quickly became apparent. Although the business was funded by his father, he was the one who had suggested the idea and later took responsibility for running it.

His father remains occupied with his professional commitments, while the young owner, who has a strong personal interest in these games, looks after the day-to-day operations.

He told me that his interest had developed through watching games, visiting different clubs and observing the kind of facilities available there.

He wanted to create a place where people could enjoy similar games and facilities without having to pay the prices usually associated with exclusive clubs and luxury hotels.

What I found particularly interesting was how involved he seemed to be with the place. After our conversation, he showed me around the different sections of the gaming lounge, as well as the coffee shops and restaurants downstairs.

He then played a few rounds with my brother and father for quite some time, and they all seemed to have a genuinely enjoyable time together. As my mother and I did not know how to play, he encouraged us to try and guided us through everything, making us feel comfortable and welcome.

Once our conversation was over, he went back to other visitors, where they were playing, and spent time talking to them. The visitors said that he sometimes join regular customers for a game.

For someone so young, seeing him move between managing the place, talking to visitors and occasionally joining them gave the gaming lounge a more personal character. It felt less like a business he owned and more like a place he genuinely enjoyed being part of.

The change Raven has undergone since opening has been significant, according to those involved with the venue. Its customer base has expanded, with students and businesspeople becoming regular visitors. Nowadays, the staff member mentioned, some band musicians with his group and friends visit here to play.

The venue also has a designated smoking area for those who prefer to smoke while taking a break from gaming. For those who want a drink between games, there is a small coffee and beverage corner inside the gaming lounge. Visitors can order coffee or other drinks without having to leave the playing area.

There are also cafes and restaurants downstairs, so players can have snacks, coffee or a proper meal without having to go elsewhere. This makes the place convenient for those who want to spend several hours there, particularly during holidays.

Raven is not simply another place to play indoor games. Its appeal lies in bringing together games that are often considered expensive leisure activities and making them available to a wider group of people.

For students, it offers an affordable way to spend time with friends. For working people, it provides an opportunity to leave the day's work behind for a while. And for those who have long enjoyed billiards, it offers a place to pursue those interests without the usual expense associated with exclusive clubs.

item.title: Boat race in Sylhet to be held on time
item.description:
The boat race on the Sonai River in Beanibazar upazila of Sylhet will be held on time next Friday (28 August), following a meeting held last night between the organisers and those opposing the event.

The race, organised by young people from Lauta and Bahadurpur villages, had faced calls for cancellation from several people campaigning under the banner of ‘Tauhidi Janata’ for a week.

They also held a meeting at the local Barigram Bazar Mosque last Thursday under the same banner and made the same demand.

When the matter was published in the media, it drew criticism.

In this situation, Beanibazar Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Umme Habiba Majumder assigned Lauta Union Chairman Delwar Hossain to resolve the matter.

‘Tauhidi Janata’ demand halt to boat race in Sylhet

Last night, a meeting was held at Baraigram market of the upazila, presided over by Delwar Hossain.

At that time, the organisers of the boat race and the opposing party were present. Later, based on everyone's consensus, it was decided to organise the boat race on time.

"The incident has been resolved by bringing both parties together," Delwar Hossain told Prothom Alo.

The boat races have been organised on the Sonai River for 15 to 20 years. 

According to the organisers, the boat race will be held in the Trigangarmukh area of the Sonai River, located between Beanibazar upazila of Sylhet and Barlekha upazila of Moulvibazar. Boats must be registered by noon next Friday to participate. The first prize will be a large cow, while the second prize will be a goat.

item.title: Starc strikes as Bangladesh struggle to stay alive against Australia
item.description:
CRICKET-AUS-BAN

An irrepressible Mitchell Starc ripped into the Bangladesh top order as Australia took an iron grip on the second Test Sunday with the visitors battling to stay alive at lunch on day two.

After 18 wickets fell on a frenetic first day in Mackay, the hosts were all out for 210 in the morning session for a lead of 146 on the back of Cameron Green's 67.

Star quick Shoriful Islam ended with 7-48 -- the best figures from a Bangladeshi bowler in an away Test.

Records galore on first day of Mackay Test

The visitors crashed for just 64 in their first innings, when Starc took 6-12, and he tormented them again to leave Bangladesh tottering at 39-3 by lunch, still 107 runs adrift.

Captain Najmul Hossain Shanto was not out 23 and Mushfiqur Rahim on four after a horror start.

Shadman Islam lasted just three balls, playing a nothing stroke to a moving Starc delivery and edging to Marnus Labuschagne at point.

Mominul Haque was equally clueless next ball, failing to offer a shot with Starc removing his off stump and setting up a hat-trick opportunity.

Starc, Shoriful take six each, Australia lead by 101 after 18-wicket day

Shanto, who was out for a golden duck in the first innings, this time survived to deny Starc.

But their woes deepened when Tanzid Hasan departed soon after for nine. Starc was again involved, taking a catch in the deep after Tanzid pulled Pat Cummins.

Australia resumed at 165-8 with Green on 51 and Nathan Lyon on 10.

Green, who scored a century during the first Test at Darwin -- which Bangladesh won by nine wickets -- kept the scoreboard moving early with quick singles.

Starc finishes with six as Bangladesh all out for 64 in first innings of second test v Australia

Lyon was first to hit a boundary with a quality drive through mid-wicket off Shoriful, but Green was also in the zone and reached the ropes twice off Hasan Mahmud in the next over.

The allrounder was undone by an inswinging yorker from the impressive Shoriful that hit him on the toe with a review declaring him out lbw.

A valiant Lyon brought up the 200 for Australia with a towering six off Taskin Ahmed and with Josh Hazlewood adding 24 crucial runs for the last wicket.

The innings ended when Hazlewood skied Taijul Islam to Shadman on six to leave Lyon not out 32.

item.title: Gas exploration cannot be halted for fear of failure
item.description:
Production at factories is being halted because of gas shortages, households are unable to cook because their stoves have no gas, vehicles are queuing for hours at CNG stations, and load-shedding is occurring frequently. The energy crisis is affecting the entire economy and people’s daily lives. What has led to this situation?

Anwar Hossain Bhuiyan:The main reason for the current energy crisis is that our gas production has declined. At the same time, imports have also been disrupted to some extent because of the war situation in the Middle East. One of the two LNG terminals in Maheshkhali, Cox’s Bazar, has developed a technical problem. Taken together, these factors mean that we are unable to supply enough gas to meet demand.

The biggest question here is why our gas production has declined. One point needs to be made: given our limited resources and manpower capacity, it can be said that the situation could have become critical much earlier if we had not been able to maintain the continuity in gas production that had existed since 2000.

However, we failed to carry out extensive exploration adequately to maintain that production. In other words, we were unable to take the right decisions at the right time when it came to the long-term planning needed to ensure gas supplies from domestic sources.

At one point, it was said that Bangladesh was “floating on gas”. Some even talked about exporting gas through pipelines. Yet the current energy crisis stems largely from dependence on imported gas. Was there no alternative to this dependence on imports?

Anwar Hossain Bhuiyan: There certainly were alternatives. The biggest alternative was to step up domestic gas exploration and strengthen the production system.

However, I do not consider the claim that “Bangladesh is floating on gas” to be realistic. I do not think any geologist would make such a statement without data, scientific analysis and evidence-based modelling. Oil and gas exploration is fraught with numerous uncertainties. Exploration activities have to be carried out while dealing with those uncertainties.

The gas fields discovered in Bangladesh are the result of long-term exploration. Our country is not very large in area. However, there are still opportunities to discover new gas through effective, science-based exploration. A great deal of work has been done in this area, but there is still much more that can be done. There are challenges, but there are also prospects for the future.

We have seen gas production decline steadily since 2016–17. Are our gas reserves running out?

Anwar Hossain Bhuiyan: Gas reserves are not infinite, nor are they renewable. So, eventually, they will run out—that is an eternal truth.

So far, we have discovered around 29 trillion cubic feet (TCF) of gas in total. Various industries have developed in our country using this gas. Alongside small and medium-sized industries, gas use has increased in the readymade garment sector, agriculture and various other areas. As a result, demand for gas has continued to rise. But we have not been able to increase supply at the same rate. This is why, after a certain point, gas production gradually began to decline.

However, we should have carried out more gas exploration. Globally, a success rate of one discovery for every eight to 10 wells drilled is considered roughly normal. In Bangladesh, the success rate is around one in three. Therefore, there is absolutely no justification for halting gas exploration for fear of failure.

By analysing seismic data, other geophysical data and information from previously drilled wells in and around our existing gas fields and in prospective areas, around 250 to 300 prospective structures have been identified.

BAPEX, some organisations under Petrobangla, multinational companies, several universities and other institutions were involved in this work. In addition, foreign consulting firms have come in at different times and analysed the data in several phases. Based on these analyses, the prospective gas fields have been ranked at various times.

How much gas could these prospective areas contain, and how long could it meet Bangladesh’s needs?

Anwar Hossain Bhuiyan: I had the opportunity to work with officials from BAPEX, Petrobangla and Sylhet Gas Fields. With their assistance, I conducted an assessment showing that around 15 TCF of gas could potentially be found in prospective areas surrounding fields where gas has already been discovered.

Suppose we drill 30 wells in the first five to seven years. If at least one-third of them are successful, we could find around five TCF of gas. If another 30 wells can be drilled over the following five years, preliminary estimates suggest that at least another five TCF could potentially be found.

In other words, if we find five TCF in the first phase and another five TCF in the next phase—ten TCF in total—our reserves, combined with the roughly eight TCF currently in hand, could reach around 18 TCF. If we can ensure an average supply of one TCF of gas a year and meet the remaining shortfall through imports, these reserves could ensure supply until 2043.

Even if drilling 30 wells yields at least five TCF of gas, its value would be around Tk five trillion (500,000 crore). By contrast, the cost of drilling 30 wells would be around Tk 75 billion (7,500 crore). Including other expenses, the total would come to Tk 100 billion (10,000 crore). In other words, the investment would be Tk 100 billion, against a potential gas value of around Tk five trillion.

It can never be considered smart management to use all our domestic gas and import not a single molecule of gas. At the same time, leaving our gas underground and becoming entirely dependent on imports is not smart management either.

We need to manage our resources in a way that ensures our domestic gas reserves remain available for a long time. That is where our bargaining power, or bargaining position, lies. You cannot negotiate with anyone when you have nothing to bargain with.We must ensure the right balance between domestic and imported gas in our energy mix.

If our gas reserves can meet our needs until 2043, other alternative energy sources will have further time to develop. Hydrocarbon reserves are gradually declining worldwide. That is why everyone is working on alternative energy sources. Research and development are under way on hydrogen energy, green energy and blue energy as well.

Given the current energy crisis, is there a possibility of any quick solutions?

Anwar Hossain Bhuiyan: I would say we should first focus on the existing gas fields. There are 29 gas fields in the country. If we consider 20 of them to be operational, there is still potential within these fields.

Due to natural geological constraints, it is not possible to extract all the gas in a field by drilling just one or a few wells. As a result, there may be some areas beyond those from which we have extracted gas where reserves remain untapped. These are known as undrained compartments.

These undrained compartments can be identified by reprocessing, reinterpreting and reevaluating data from existing gas fields. New wells can then be drilled there quickly. Since gas has already been found in another part of the same field, the likelihood of finding gas in these areas is relatively high. Another major advantage is that there would be no need to build new infrastructure. Existing infrastructure could be used, allowing gas to be supplied directly to the national grid. This could be a quick and effective way to increase gas production.

Oil and gas exploration began in Bangladesh in 1955 and became a reality with discoveries in 1961. As a result, many of our wells are quite old. Many of these wells have deteriorated. Production can be increased by repairing them through workovers.

However, everyone should remember that whether it is BAPEX or a foreign company, all parties involved in exploration have to work amid considerable uncertainty.

Bangladesh is a small country, and our gas fields are also relatively small. So exploration failures should not be viewed as a major setback. Rather, failing to find gas in a well means we have gained new information. That information is extremely valuable. It can be used to make future exploration more precise and reduce uncertainty.

Another possibility is to drill into the deeper sections of gas fields that are currently in production. Because of our technological limitations, we have so far drilled only to certain depths and extracted gas from the upper layers. But the layers deeper below offer not only uncertainty but also a much greater possibility of finding gas.

Bangladesh has already taken initiatives for deep drilling in several gas fields. I believe these fields could yield some very encouraging results.

In short, by identifying undrained compartments and drilling new wells, repairing existing wells through workovers to increase production, and drilling into deeper layers of existing gas fields, we can increase production from the fields we already have.

How likely are we to discover new gas fields?

Anwar Hossain Bhuiyan: There is potential in under-explored or unexplored areas between existing gas fields. As gas fields are found around structures such as Titas, Bakhrabad and Bibiyana, the potential in the intervening areas is not zero.

Another important prospective area is the hinge zone. This transitional zone, stretching from Kolkata through Pabna and Mymensingh to Sylhet, has seen relatively little exploration. The recent discovery of gas in Jamalpur indicates the potential of this region. Further exploration will be needed to determine whether the gas in Jamalpur can be commercially extracted.

Then there is the extensive area of the Sylhet Trough or Surma Basin, as well as the Hatiya Trough and its surrounding areas. Cumilla, Brahmanbaria and Sylhet are the country’s main hydrocarbon hubs. Meanwhile, the presence of hydrocarbons in the Hatiya Trough region has been established through gas discoveries at Shahbazpur, Bhola North, Sundarpur, Feni, and offshore at Sangu and Kutubdia. However, these areas have not been studied or researched sufficiently. With detailed studies and exploration, this could become the country’s second major hydrocarbon hub.

However, extensive exploration and drilling will be required in these prospective areas. It is natural that many of these wells will turn out to be dry holes. Therefore, exploration should be pursued as part of a long-term plan rather than being viewed as a loss.

Gas has been discovered in Tripura, India. How much potential is there for gas in the Chittagong Hill Tracts? What are the challenges of exploration there?

Anwar Hossain Bhuiyan: The geological structure of the Chittagong Hill Tracts is highly complex. As a result, oil and gas exploration in this region is relatively challenging. India’s Tripura state has a similar geological structure nearby. Tripura covers around 10,000 square kilometres, while Chattogram and the Chittagong Hill Tracts together cover around 18,000 square kilometres. Tripura has around 14 structures, while we have 28.

More than 150 exploration wells have been drilled in Tripura. So far, around 2.7 trillion cubic feet (TCF) of proven gas reserves have been identified there, and according to their estimates, there is potential for at least 14 TCF of gas. Importantly, they did not stop exploration despite the failures they encountered.

There are many similarities between the geological structures of Tripura and the Chittagong Hill Tracts. If they were able to begin exploration later and achieve success, the possibility of finding gas in our Chittagong Hill Tracts cannot be ruled out either.

The maritime boundary disputes with India and Myanmar were settled a decade ago. How much gas could potentially be found in our vast maritime area? Why has there been no effective initiative to explore for gas offshore?

Anwar Hossain Bhuiyan: I would explain this challenge from the perspective of a rather harsh reality. Major multinational companies conduct exploration in the maritime areas of Brazil, Angola, Mexico and the Middle East. Large reserves are often found in a single gas field in these areas.

Companies that invest billions of dollars in Bangladesh’s maritime area would naturally expect substantial returns. So how do you attract them? By demonstrating success, of course. This creates a kind of ‘chicken-and-egg’ problem. Should we explore first and demonstrate success, and then attract foreign companies? Or should they come first, and then we explore?

If we can demonstrate success, they will come. But if they do not come, we currently lack the capacity to undertake large-scale exploration and demonstrate that success ourselves.

Although there has yet to be any major success in oil and gas exploration in Bangladesh’s deep sea, there are reasons to remain hopeful. In particular, gas discoveries in Myanmar, along with certain geological similarities with Bangladesh’s offshore area, point to potential. In some parts of our maritime area, sedimentary rocks extend to depths of 17 to 19 kilometres. There is potential for oil and gas to have formed, accumulated and become trapped in these deep layers. Moreover, the deeper offshore region contains the world’s largest deep-sea fan—the Bengal Fan.

However, the challenges will remain until success is achieved. To generate interest among international companies and encourage investment, we must do the necessary work ourselves—particularly by properly analysing existing seismic data, identifying prospects and ensuring investment-friendly policies.

There have long been calls to build national capacity in gas exploration and production. BAPEX has achieved greater success in gas exploration with limited resources. How can BAPEX’s capacity be strengthened?

Anwar Hossain Bhuiyan: Two factors are important in explaining why BAPEX’s capabilities have not reached international standards. First, talented engineers and geologists who join BAPEX gain experience and develop expertise at an international level. But when they see that a friend with the same skills is working for a foreign company for much higher pay and benefits, they become frustrated.

As a result, many leave the country in search of better opportunities. This is a form of ‘brain drain’. Therefore, at the national level, we should consider providing BAPEX’s skilled personnel with special benefits to retain them.

Second, strengthening capacity requires investment in new technologies and modern software, rigs and drilling technology, as well as the ability to acquire two-dimensional and three-dimensional seismic data. In other words, capacity must be built through a combination of skilled personnel, software and hardware.

One might now ask, we are already doing, or trying to do, these things. So why is it still not enough? The reality is that investment is inadequate. We are spending billions of taka on energy imports. The subsidies we had to provide for buying gas from the spot market during the Covid-19 pandemic may have been more than ten times what was invested in gas exploration and capacity building over the past decade. It is not possible to build substantial capacity with such limited investment.

Therefore, if we are to make a long-term plan, we cannot consider only how much we are investing at present. We must consider both what will happen if we do not invest and what the potential returns could be if we succeed.

We must also move away from the mindset that a dry hole or an unsuccessful exploration attempt in one location means everything is over. Failure is inevitable in exploration. The information gained from that failure can also be extremely valuable for subsequent exploration. Therefore, failing to find gas in a well should not be viewed simply as a loss, but also as an opportunity to gain new information for future exploration.

item.title: Dangerous trap of mobile phone loans
item.description:
Private sector employee Shaheen Hossain borrowed Tk 6,000 Taka in three phases via a mobile app last June. For this short-term loan, he ended up repaying nearly Tk 10,000, implying an interest rate of 800 per cent.

Shaheen Hossain told Prothom Alo that he refused to pay as the app demanded more money. He then received threats on WhatsApp stating that his personal information stored on his phone would be leaked and his relatives would be contacted.

He said, "The interest kept increasing daily, and I was receiving threats. Eventually, I repaid the money and swore never to take a loan like this again."

The app Shaheen used was called FinCash. Prothom Alo has identified 30 such apps operating in Bangladesh, despite being illegal.

According to victims’ accounts and reports published in the media in several South Asian countries, the operators of these apps advertise on Facebook and other social media platforms to lure users. When someone downloads an app to take out a loan, it accesses and collects various data from the person’s mobile phone without their knowledge, including photos, videos, contact numbers and text messages. The operators then demand high interest on the loans. Those who fail to repay face harassment.

While this trend is new and hasn't spread widely in Bangladesh, the media from India, Pakistan, and other South Asian countries reports that it has taken a dangerous turn there.

According to a 12 December 2024 report by Indian media outlet NDTV, a young man named Narendra (25) from Andhra Pradesh took a 2,000 Rupee loan from an app after his wedding. He was asked for an excessive repayment amount, which he refused to pay, leading to harassment. At one point, he was threatened with the distribution of distorted images of his bride.

The NDTV report further stated that Narendra ultimately committed suicide, another tragic incident resulting from harassment by these illegal loan apps that have mushroomed in India.

App lending is Illegal

In Bangladesh, loans are legally provided by banks, financial institutions, and microcredit organisations. Informal loans secured by pledging gold jewelry are common, as well as mahajani (moneylender) loans.

According to Bangladesh Bank, as of last June, the private sector has outstanding loans amounting to Tk 18. 25 trillion in the banking system.

The Microcredit Regulatory Authority (MRA) reported that as of June 2024, the microloan balance was Tk 2. 62 trillion.

Currently, BRAC Bank, Dhaka Bank, and Prime Bank are offering loans via apps. Mobile Financial Service (MFS) provider bKash also provides app-based loans in partnership with City Bank.

Despite this large loan market, there is demand for urgent and easy loans at the individual level. Various apps are exploiting this opportunity, even though unauthorised loans, online gambling, unauthorised currency exchange or forex trading, and cryptocurrency (a type of digital currency) transactions are prohibited in the country. Financial transaction service platforms cannot be operated by unregistered entities, yet there are ongoing operations of app-based loans, gambling, and forex trading.

When asked, Arif Hossain Khan, spokesperson for Bangladesh Bank, told Prothom Alo he wasn't aware of illegal loan apps. The central bank will take all necessary initiatives to raise awareness among people about the frauds of digital loan apps.

Identifying 30 Apps

By reviewing Facebook ads and Google Play Store, at least 30 apps conducting loan activities in Bangladesh have been identified. These apps carry various names like Bongo Cash, Dhaka Fin, Taka Now, Easy Taka, Fin Cash, Sathi Loan, Asha Loan, Suvidha Loan, etc. Some apps slyly use well-known microcredit organisations' names.

For instance, an app named Sathi Loan offers personal loans up to Tk 150, 000 with interest ranging from 18-26 per cent annually. This app appeared in the Google Play Store in February this year and has been downloaded over a hundred thousand times.

Another app named ''Quick Loan'' offers loans up to Tk 300,000 at 18 per cent interest. The app launched on the Play Store in September last year and has been downloaded over half a million times.

One of the victims of harassment after borrowing from an app is Saeed Mia from Mirpur, Dhaka. Before Eid-ul-Azha, he couldn't withdraw cash from several ATMs, and in urgent need, he applied for a loan from an app advertised on Facebook.

Saeed Mia told Prothom Alo that he took a total of Tk 24,000 in loans, yet after just a week, the app showed arrears of Tk 81,000 with interest. He repaid Tk 54,000. He complained that upon refusing to pay the remainder, his acquaintances were called and threatened.

Victims shared that while applying for the loan, they were asked for images of their National ID cards (NIDs) and phone numbers linked to financial services (bKash, Nagad, etc.). The money was sent to their mobile financial service numbers.

The loan application process required installing the app on the mobile phone. The app sought permission to access the phonebook, photos, messages, and location data, failing which it would not operate.

Mirpur's victim Saeed Mia mentioned that during the app installation, he had to grant access to various phone data, later realising that all numbers and information on his phone went to the app operators.

The growing usage of these loan apps in Bangladesh is evident from data by web traffic analyzer SimilarWeb. The website lists Bitcoin, online trading, and loan apps among popular finance apps in Bangladesh.

Who runs these apps

The operators of these apps have no office or address. There is no information on who runs them or from where.

A statement from the US Department of Justice in April revealed the existence of online scam syndicates near the Cambodian, Laos, and Myanmar border. Citing UN data, the statement mentioned that by the end of 2023, the conservative estimate of annual financial theft by these syndicates worldwide would reach around $640 billion (approximately Tk 8 trillion).

The Indian government has recently initiated actions against these illegal loan apps. According to an NDTV report on 12 August, as of June, India had shut down 3,718 apps.

Prothom Alo spoke with five victims. One of them lodged a complaint via email with a police agency. The others did not even do that. The Criminal Investigation Department (CID) and detective branch (DB) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police claim they have received no complaints or cases.

Analysts stress the need to act before such fraud reaches a critical level in Bangladesh; otherwise, there is a risk of significant losses to individuals and increased money laundering.

Professor BM Moinul Hossain from the Institute of Information Technology at Dhaka University told Prothom Alo that these crimes continue in evolving forms. A lack of user awareness, irresponsible platforms, and ineffective action by law enforcement and regulatory bodies are equally to blame.

item.title: Four family members found dead in Rangpur home
item.description:
Police have recovered the bodies of four members of a family, including a retired schoolteacher and his wife, from their home in Kamalkashana Masua Para Mohalla in Rangpur city.
The bodies of retired Rangpur District School teacher Ganapati Chakraborty, 65, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty, 50, daughter Kandi Chakraborty, 24, and son Priyam Chakraborty, 12, were recovered from the locked house at around 11:45pm on Saturday.
Rangpur Metropolitan Kotwali police station OC Nazmul Alam confirmed the recovery of the four bodies.
According to police and local residents, the door to Ganapati’s house had remained locked for the past two days. Relatives became suspicious after repeated phone calls to the family went unanswered.
At around 10:45pm on Saturday, locals informed the fire service, which broke open the door and entered the house. Two bodies were found inside, while two others were recovered near the roof, according to police.
After receiving the information, Rangpur Metropolitan Detective Branch Deputy Commissioner Sanatan Chakraborty, Kotwali police station OC Nazmul Islam and other police officials, along with a RAB team, cordoned off the house.
Relatives alleged that the four family members had been murdered and demanded that those responsible be arrested and brought to justice.
They also suspected that the family may have been killed after confronting robbers. Household items were found scattered, and jewellery boxes inside a cupboard appeared to have been disturbed, prompting relatives to suspect that cash and gold ornaments may have been looted.
Malti Chakraborty, a cousin of Ganapati, alleged that the deaths were the result of a planned murder and demanded a proper investigation.
Rangpur Metropolitan Police Deputy Commissioner Sanatan Chakraborty said the matter was being investigated.
"We have recovered the bodies of four people. They will be sent to the Rangpur Medical College Hospital morgue for autopsies. Necessary legal action is being taken after identifying those involved," he said.
Police are investigating the possible cause and motive behind the deaths, he added.

item.title: Bangladeshi sailor among 2 rescued after ship sinks off Odisha
item.description:
A Bangladeshi sailor was among two crew members rescued after a Panama-flagged bulk carrier carrying 24 sailors sank in the Bay of Bengal, around 240 nautical miles off Paradip, Odisha, India, on Saturday.
The Indian Coast Guard (ICG) said the two sailors were rescued alive from liferafts, while a search and rescue operation is underway for the remaining 22 crew members.
Indian media outlet India Today reported the incident on Sunday.
The vessel, MV Ocean Winner, was carrying 20 Chinese, three Myanmar and one Bangladeshi national, according to the ICG.
The ship had last anchored at Paradip Port and was bound for Singapore with a cargo of iron ore.
The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre (MRCC) of the Indian Coast Guard received a report from the company operating the vessel at around 11:48am after contact with MV Ocean Winner was lost. The company requested an immediate search and rescue operation.
Following the report, the MRCC directed a nearby commercial vessel, MT Isopos, to search for the missing vessel and its liferafts.
At around 8pm, MT Isopos rescued two sailors from two liferafts, the ICG said. Their physical condition was not immediately known.
The Indian Coast Guard and Navy have launched a joint operation to locate the remaining sailors. ICG vessels Barad and Anmol have been deployed, while another vessel, Vijit, was dispatched from Sri Vijaya Puram to strengthen the search.
Authorities are also coordinating with other vessels in the area to locate the remaining sailors and liferafts.
The cause of the vessel’s sinking has not yet been confirmed.
Further details on the rescued sailors and the condition of the remaining crew are awaited as the search operation continues.
